title: Look to tomorrow
hook: let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (59:18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ithar, and your line was others first. What did you give away without mentioning it? Day six hundred nineteen.

Before a long trip, people send things ahead. A box shipped to the new address. A deposit on the apartment. A message to a friend at the other end: I land Thursday. When they arrive, what's waiting for them is exactly what they sent. Nothing more. Surah Al-Hashr, near its end, turns from the story of Medina to a single soul, and asks it to do what every traveler does the night before leaving: check what's already been sent on ahead.

Verse eighteen. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Observe your duty to Allah. And let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow." The word for tomorrow is ghad, the ordinary word for the day after today. Many commentators said it here means the Day of Judgment, and asked why it's called tomorrow. Their answer: because it's so certain and so near that it's as close as tomorrow is. The verb is qaddamat, what it has sent forward, put ahead of itself. Deeds are pictured as things you ship on before you. Notice that the command to be mindful of God, taqwa, comes twice, at the start and again after the question, like bookends. And the next verse warns: don't be like those who forgot God, so that God made them forget their own selves. Forgetting God and forgetting yourself are tied together. Hadith give the shipping list. Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said when a person dies, their deeds stop, except three: an ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits others, and a righteous child who prays for them. Three things that keep arriving after you've gone. And a report in Tirmidhi shows how upside down the accounting is. The family once slaughtered a sheep and gave nearly all of it away. 'A'isha told the Prophet that only the shoulder was left. He answered: all of it is left, except its shoulder. What you keep is spent. What you send ahead stays.
screen: `GHAD: TOMORROW, SO NEAR.` · `QADDAMAT: WHAT IT SENT AHEAD.` · `THREE THINGS THAT KEEP ARRIVING.` · `ALL OF IT REMAINS BUT THE SHOULDER.`

segments.voice: The practice: do one thing for your future self. Sit, and breathe. Picture yourself a year from now, looking back on today. What would that person thank you for? A kindness that outlasts the day, a small amount given, something learned and passed on, a call to a parent. Choose one. Then ask today's line quietly: what have I sent ahead? Let the answer be small and real. The bell holds the time.
Look to tomorrow. Let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, Surah Al-Hashr says, with taqwa on either side. Today's word.
Your line: what have I sent ahead? Today, do your one thing for the year-from-now you, and give away one thing you'd have kept. Day six hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims often recite 59:18 in Friday sermons as a call to self-reckoning, muhasaba, and many set up ongoing charities, sadaqa jariya, such as wells, schools or copies of the Qur'an, hoping their reward continues after death.

fork.setup: the family has given away a whole sheep except the shoulder. 'A'isha says only the shoulder is left. what does the Prophet answer?
options: all of it remains, except its shoulder.
fork.reveal: what was given away is what remains; what you keep is what's used up.

original.note: Arabic: what it has sent ahead for tomorrow. ghad is the everyday word for tomorrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse about planning for the future.
what it means: every soul checking what it has sent on ahead, for a tomorrow that's nearer than it looks.
what a scholar hears: ghad read as the Day of Judgment for its nearness; taqwa repeated as bookends; 59:19 links forgetting God with forgetting the self; Muslim 1631 and Tirmidhi 2470.
